content: Cardiotocography (CTG) is a method used to monitor the fetal heart rate in relation to maternal uterine contractions during labor. Despite the existence of guidelines for interpreting CTG, there is significant variability in how maternity care providers interpret these readings, both between different observers and even by the same observer at different times. Misinterpretation of CTG data can lead to poor clinical decisions, which may result in unnecessary interventions or delays in necessary treatments. Expert systems (ESs), a form of applied artificial intelligence, have the potential to assist in complex clinical decision-making and improve the interpretation of fetal heart rate tracings. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of continuous or intermittent CTG monitoring during labor when used in conjunction with an ES. This was compared to either (1) CTG monitoring without an ES or (2) intermittent auscultation using a Pinard stethoscope or a hand-held Doppler ultrasound device. The outcomes of interest included perinatal mortality, cesarean delivery, operative vaginal birth, fetal blood sampling, artificial rupture of membranes, oxytocin augmentation of labor, maternal satisfaction, neonatal seizures, fetal acidaemia, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, admission to neonatal special care or intensive care units, and Apgar scores below seven at five minutes. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, Open Grey, and ProQuest Dissertation & Theses Database, as well as reference lists of relevant studies. The search was completed in October 2014. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing CTG monitoring with an ES to CTG monitoring without an ES, or to intermittent auscultation, were eligible for inclusion. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted data to ensure accuracy. The authors of the included trials were contacted to clarify unclear aspects of the study designs. No studies were identified that compared CTG monitoring with an ES to intermittent auscultation. However, two randomized controlled trials comparing CTG monitoring with an ES to CTG monitoring without an ES were included in the qualitative synthesis. Only one of these trials, involving 220 participants, provided data for quantitative analysis. Both trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias. The results showed no strong evidence that CTG monitoring with an ES reduced the incidence of cesarean delivery (risk ratio [RR] 0.61; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.35 to 1.04) compared to CTG monitoring with fetal blood sampling. Similarly, there was no strong evidence to suggest a reduction in neonatal seizures (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.01 to 8.09) or fetal acidaemia (RR 0.50; 95% CI 0.09 to 2.67) when using CTG with an ES versus CTG without an ES. Perinatal mortality could not be evaluated in this trial due to the lack of data on early neonatal deaths. While fetal deaths were recorded, no fetal deaths occurred in either group, preventing the calculation of risk estimates. There was also no strong evidence to support a reduction in the incidence of forceps-assisted vaginal births (RR 0.50; 95% CI 0.05 to 5.43), hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.01 to 8.09), neonatal intensive care unit admissions (RR 0.40; 95% CI 0.08 to 2.02), or Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (RR 0.50; 95% CI 0.13 to 1.95). The trial did not report on outcomes such as artificial rupture of membranes, oxytocin augmentation of labor, or maternal satisfaction with labor. In conclusion, while two trials met the inclusion criteria for this review, only one trial provided data for analysis, and it was underpowered to evaluate the primary outcomes of interest. As a result, no clinical recommendations can currently be made regarding the use of ESs for fetal assessment during labor. Further adequately powered trials are needed to determine the impact of ESs on fetal assessment and labor outcomes.
